title: UNIT 6: HYDROCARBONS AND THEIR NATURAL SOURCES
notes:
✓ Hydrocarbons → Organic compounds made only of carbon and hydrogen.

→ They include saturated hydrocarbons such as alkanes and unsaturated hydrocarbons such as alkenes and alkynes. Important aromatic hydrocarbons include benzene.

✓ Major natural sources → Petroleum, crude oil, natural gas and biogas.

title: 6.1 Organic and Inorganic Compounds
notes:
✓ Organic compounds → Mainly carbon-containing compounds, usually containing C–H bonds. Examples include hydrocarbons, alcohols, aldehydes and carboxylic acids.

✓ Inorganic compounds → Generally do not contain C–H bonds. Examples include NaCl, H₂O and CO₂.

title: 6.1.1 Life Force (Vitalism) Theory
notes:
✓ Vitalism → The old idea that organic compounds could only be produced by living organisms because they required a special life force.

→ The theory was disproved when organic compounds were successfully prepared from inorganic substances, showing that organic compounds can be synthesized in the laboratory.

title: 6.1.2 Homologous Series
notes:
✓ Homologous series → A family of organic compounds with the same functional group and general formula, in which successive members differ by –CH₂–.

→ Members have similar chemical properties but gradually changing physical properties.

◆ EXAMPLE: ALKANES
CH₄ → C₂H₆ → C₃H₈ → C₄H₁₀

title: 6.1.3 Functional Group
notes:
✓ Functional group → An atom or group of atoms responsible for the characteristic chemical reactions of an organic compound.

◆ EXAMPLES
✓ –OH → Alcohol.
✓ –COOH → Carboxylic acid.
✓ –CO– → Ketone.
✓ –X → Alkyl halide.

title: 6.1.4 Isomers
notes:
✓ Isomers → Compounds that have the same molecular formula but different structural arrangements or spatial arrangements of atoms.

◆ MAIN TYPES
✓ Chain isomerism.
✓ Position isomerism.
✓ Geometrical isomerism.

title: 6.1.5 Chain Isomerism
notes:
✓ Chain isomerism → Occurs when compounds have the same molecular formula but different arrangements of the carbon skeleton.

◆ EXAMPLE
C₄H₁₀ → n-butane and 2-methylpropane.

title: 6.1.6 Position Isomerism
notes:
✓ Position isomerism → Occurs when compounds have the same carbon skeleton and functional group but the functional group, multiple bond or substituent is located at different positions.

◆ EXAMPLE
1-propanol and 2-propanol.

title: 6.1.7 Geometrical Isomerism
notes:
✓ Geometrical isomerism → Occurs because rotation around a carbon-carbon double bond is restricted.

◆ TYPES
✓ cis-isomer → Similar groups on the same side.
✓ trans-isomer → Similar groups on opposite sides.

→ It is common in suitably substituted alkenes.

title: 6.2 Saturated Hydrocarbons: Alkanes
notes:
✓ Alkanes → Saturated hydrocarbons containing only carbon-carbon single bonds.

◆ GENERAL FORMULA
CₙH₂ₙ₊₂

◆ EXAMPLES
✓ CH₄ → Methane.
✓ C₂H₆ → Ethane.
✓ C₃H₈ → Propane.

→ They are relatively unreactive and mainly undergo combustion and substitution reactions.

title: 6.2.1 Alkyl Radicals
notes:
✓ Alkyl group → Formed by removing one hydrogen atom from an alkane.

◆ GENERAL FORMULA
CₙH₂ₙ₊₁–

◆ EXAMPLES
✓ CH₃– → Methyl.
✓ C₂H₅– → Ethyl.
✓ C₃H₇– → Propyl.

→ Alkyl groups commonly occur as substituents in organic compounds.

title: 6.2.2 Substitution Reaction
notes:
✓ Substitution reaction → A reaction in which one atom or group in a compound is replaced by another atom or group.

→ Alkanes commonly undergo substitution with halogens in the presence of light.

◆ EXAMPLE
CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl

title: 6.2.3 Halogenation
notes:
✓ Halogenation → The introduction of a halogen atom into an organic compound.

→ Alkanes undergo halogenation by substitution, usually in the presence of ultraviolet light.

◆ EXAMPLE
CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl

title: 6.3 Unsaturated Hydrocarbons
notes:
✓ Unsaturated hydrocarbons → Hydrocarbons containing at least one carbon-carbon multiple bond.

◆ TYPES
✓ Alkenes → Contain C=C.
✓ Alkynes → Contain C≡C.

→ They are generally more reactive than alkanes and commonly undergo addition reactions.

title: 6.3.1 Alkenes
notes:
✓ Alkenes → Unsaturated hydrocarbons containing at least one carbon-carbon double bond.

◆ GENERAL FORMULA FOR SIMPLE ACYCLIC ALKENES
CₙH₂ₙ

◆ EXAMPLES
✓ C₂H₄ → Ethene.
✓ C₃H₆ → Propene.

→ They commonly undergo addition and polymerization reactions.

title: 6.3.2 Alkynes
notes:
✓ Alkynes → Unsaturated hydrocarbons containing at least one carbon-carbon triple bond.

◆ GENERAL FORMULA FOR SIMPLE ACYCLIC ALKYNES
CₙH₂ₙ₋₂

◆ EXAMPLE
C₂H₂ → Ethyne.

→ They undergo addition reactions because of the triple bond.

title: 6.3.3 Addition Reaction
notes:
✓ Addition reaction → Occurs when atoms or groups are added across a carbon-carbon double or triple bond, producing a single product.

◆ EXAMPLES
✓ Alkene + H₂ → Alkane.
✓ Alkene + Br₂ → Dibromoalkane.
✓ Alkene + HCl → Chloroalkane.

→ Addition reactions are characteristic of unsaturated hydrocarbons.

title: 6.3.4 Hydrohalogenation
notes:
✓ Hydrohalogenation → The addition of a hydrogen halide such as HCl, HBr or HI across a carbon-carbon double bond.

◆ EXAMPLE
CH₂=CH₂ + HCl → CH₃CH₂Cl

→ The reaction converts an alkene into an alkyl halide.

title: 6.3.5 Markovnikov's Rule
notes:
✓ Markovnikov's rule → Predicts the major product when an unsymmetrical alkene reacts with a hydrogen halide.

→ The hydrogen attaches to the double-bond carbon that already has more hydrogen atoms, while the halide attaches to the carbon with fewer hydrogen atoms.

◆ REMEMBER
→ H goes to the carbon with more H.

title: 6.3.6 Alkyl Halides
notes:
✓ Alkyl halides → Organic compounds in which a halogen atom is bonded to an alkyl group.

◆ GENERAL FORM
R–X

✓ X = F, Cl, Br or I.

◆ EXAMPLES
✓ CH₃Cl → Chloromethane.
✓ C₂H₅Br → Bromoethane.

→ They can undergo substitution and elimination reactions.

title: 6.3.7 Elimination Reaction
notes:
✓ Elimination reaction → A reaction that removes atoms or groups from a molecule to form a multiple bond.

◆ EXAMPLE
CH₃CH₂Br → CH₂=CH₂ + HBr

→ Elimination reactions are commonly used to prepare alkenes from alkyl halides.

title: 6.3.8 Dehydrohalogenation
notes:
✓ Dehydrohalogenation → An elimination reaction in which hydrogen halide is removed from an alkyl halide to form an alkene.

◆ EXAMPLE
CH₃CH₂Br → CH₂=CH₂ + HBr

→ It is commonly carried out using an alcoholic base and heat.

title: 6.3.9 Hydrogenation
notes:
✓ Hydrogenation → The addition of hydrogen to an unsaturated compound in the presence of a catalyst such as Ni, Pt or Pd.

◆ EXAMPLE
CH₂=CH₂ + H₂ → CH₃CH₃

→ It converts unsaturated hydrocarbons into more saturated compounds.

title: 6.3.10 Polymerization
notes:
✓ Polymerization → The joining of many small molecules called monomers to form a large molecule called a polymer.

→ Alkenes can undergo addition polymerization.

◆ EXAMPLE
nCH₂=CH₂ → (–CH₂–CH₂–)ₙ

Ethene → Polyethylene.

title: 6.3.11 Cracking
notes:
✓ Cracking → The breaking of large hydrocarbon molecules into smaller hydrocarbons by heat, usually with a catalyst.

→ It produces useful smaller alkanes and alkenes.

◆ GENERAL EXAMPLE
Large alkane → Smaller alkane + Alkene.

→ Cracking increases the supply of useful fuels and raw materials for petrochemical industries.

title: 6.3.12 Wurtz Reaction
notes:
✓ Wurtz reaction → Used to prepare higher alkanes by reacting alkyl halides with sodium metal in dry ether.

◆ GENERAL REACTION
2R–X + 2Na → R–R + 2NaX

◆ EXAMPLE
2CH₃Cl + 2Na → C₂H₆ + 2NaCl

title: 6.3.13 Decarboxylation
notes:
✓ Decarboxylation → The removal of carbon dioxide from a carboxylic acid or its salt.

→ Sodium salts of carboxylic acids can be heated with soda lime to produce an alkane containing one fewer carbon atom.

◆ EXAMPLE
CH₃COONa + NaOH → CH₄ + Na₂CO₃

title: 6.3.14 Cycloalkanes and Cycloalkenes
notes:
✓ Cycloalkanes → Saturated hydrocarbons containing carbon atoms arranged in a ring.

◆ GENERAL FORMULA FOR SIMPLE MONOCYCLIC CYCLOALKANES
CₙH₂ₙ

✓ Cycloalkenes → Cyclic hydrocarbons containing at least one carbon-carbon double bond.

◆ EXAMPLES
✓ Cyclopropane → Cycloalkane.
✓ Cyclohexene → Cycloalkene.

title: 6.4 Aromatic Hydrocarbon: Benzene
notes:
✓ Benzene (C₆H₆) → The simplest aromatic hydrocarbon. It has a six-carbon ring with delocalized electrons.

◆ PROPERTIES
✓ Colorless liquid.
✓ Volatile and flammable.
✓ Relatively stable because of aromaticity.

→ Benzene mainly undergoes substitution reactions rather than ordinary addition reactions.

title: 6.4.1 Carboxylic Acid and Ketone
notes:
✓ Carboxylic acids → Contain the –COOH functional group.

◆ GENERAL FORM
R–COOH

◆ EXAMPLE
CH₃COOH → Ethanoic acid.

✓ Ketones → Contain a carbonyl group within the carbon chain.

◆ GENERAL FORM
R–CO–R′

◆ EXAMPLE
CH₃COCH₃ → Propanone.

title: 6.5 Petroleum and Crude Oil
notes:
✓ Petroleum → A naturally occurring mixture of hydrocarbons found beneath Earth's surface.
✓ Crude oil → The unrefined liquid petroleum obtained from underground deposits.

→ Crude oil is separated by fractional distillation into fractions with different boiling ranges.

◆ MAJOR FRACTIONS
✓ Refinery gases.
✓ Gasoline.
✓ Kerosene.
✓ Diesel oil.
✓ Lubricating oils.
✓ Fuel oil.
✓ Bitumen.

title: 6.5.1 Natural Gas
notes:
✓ Natural gas → A gaseous fossil fuel found underground, often associated with petroleum deposits.

→ Its main component is methane (CH₄), with smaller amounts of other hydrocarbons.

◆ USES
✓ Cooking.
✓ Heating.
✓ Electricity generation.
✓ Production of hydrogen and chemicals.

title: 6.5.2 Biogas
notes:
✓ Biogas → A mixture of gases produced by anaerobic decomposition of organic matter by microorganisms.

✓ Main component → Methane (CH₄).
✓ Other component → Carbon dioxide (CO₂).

◆ SOURCES
✓ Animal manure.
✓ Sewage.
✓ Organic waste.

◆ USES
✓ Cooking.
✓ Heating.
✓ Electricity generation.

title: 6.5.3 Destructive Distillation
notes:
✓ Destructive distillation → The heating of an organic substance strongly in the absence or limited supply of air, causing it to decompose into simpler products.

◆ EXAMPLE
Coal can produce coke, coal gas, coal tar and other products.

→ It differs from ordinary distillation because chemical decomposition occurs.

title: UNIT MUST REMEMBER
notes:
◆ HYDROCARBONS
✓ Hydrocarbons → Compounds containing only C and H.

✓ Alkanes → Saturated; CₙH₂ₙ₊₂; mainly substitution.
✓ Alkenes → C=C; CₙH₂ₙ; mainly addition.
✓ Alkynes → C≡C; CₙH₂ₙ₋₂; addition reactions.
✓ Benzene → Aromatic hydrocarbon; mainly substitution.

◆ ORGANIC REACTIONS
✓ Addition → Atoms/groups add across multiple bonds.
✓ Substitution → One atom/group replaces another.
✓ Elimination → Atoms/groups are removed to form a multiple bond.
✓ Hydrogenation → Addition of H₂.
✓ Hydrohalogenation → Addition of HX.
✓ Dehydrohalogenation → Removal of HX.
✓ Polymerization → Monomers form polymers.
✓ Cracking → Large hydrocarbons break into smaller ones.
✓ Wurtz → Alkyl halide + Na → Higher alkane.

◆ NATURAL SOURCES
✓ Petroleum/crude oil → Mixture of hydrocarbons.
✓ Natural gas → Mainly methane.
✓ Biogas → Mainly methane + CO₂.

◆ EXAM TIP
✓ Saturated → Single bonds.
✓ Unsaturated → Double/triple bonds.
✓ Alkane → Substitution.
✓ Alkene/alkyne → Addition.
✓ Benzene → Substitution.
✓ Markovnikov → H goes to the carbon already having more H.
